query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface fluorination treatment (via a dilute NH4F spray) on an Al-containing refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3-based protective scale at high temperatures, thereby markedly reducing oxidation‐induced weight gain compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An Al-bearing refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) typically formulated with refractory elements (e.g., Nb, Ta, Mo) and an oxidation‐promoting amount of Al for structural applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a dilute NH4F solution via spraying to the alloy surface (i.e. a surface fluorination treatment).
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in flowing dry air at around 1000 °C for extended durations (e.g., up to 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 (and possibly mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The fluorine treatment is expected to induce the formation of aluminum fluoride intermediates at the surface that, upon exposure to high-temperature oxygen, decompose to yield a protective Al2O3 film. This selective oxidation process suppresses the rapid formation of less protective oxides (such as TiO2 or unprotected refractory oxides) by enhancing local Al oxidation kinetics, similar to the fluorine effect demonstrated in TiAl alloys, while also complementing the known benefits of Al additions in RHEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an untreated RHEA, the fluorine-treated alloy will show a substantially lower weight gain (by a similar order of magnitude as seen in previous fluorine-treated TiAl alloys) and a more uniform, adherent oxide scale after 100 hours at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys with comparable compositions typically develop nonuniform, less protective oxide scales and higher oxidation-induced weight gains under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: This benefit is anticipated for RHEAs that contain a sufficient Al content to form Al2O3; if the alloy has very low Al or if the operating temperature is significantly higher than 1100 °C (where other degradation mechanisms may dominate), the fluorine treatment may not yield the predicted improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates the fluorine-induced selective oxidation effect observed in γ-TiAl (evidence from PMC9030595::web::000::abstract and PMC9030595::web::017::4_conclusions) to Al-containing RHEAs (supported by oxidation studies in RHEAs such as PMC6513993::web::000::abstract). The new aspect is applying this surface treatment to a refractory high-entropy alloy system, and the precise magnitude of weight gain reduction is uncertain since the underlying diffusion and reaction kinetics in RHEAs may differ.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an Al-containing RHEA: one group undergoes the dilute NH4F surface treatment and the other remains untreated. Subject both groups to isothermal oxidation in flowing dry air at 1000 °C for 100 hours.
measurements: Measure weight gain per unit area (mg/cm²) over time using thermogravimetric analysis.
Characterize the surface oxide scale via SEM, EDS, and XRD to assess continuity, phase composition (specifically, the presence of continuous Al2O3), and adhesion.
Compare the oxidation kinetics (parabolic rate constants) between treated and untreated samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and fail to form a more continuous and adherent Al2O3-based scale relative to untreated samples, or if the oxide scale microstructure does not differ markedly from that of the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
